8.8 Estimating Average Reservoir Pressure
Two different method types, one using data from the middle-time region and the second using
data  from  the  late-time  region  (LTR),  are  commonly  applied  in  estimating  average  reservoir
pressure. The middle-time region methods are the Matthews-Brons-Hazebroek (MBH) method20
and the Ramey-Cobb method.24 The LTR methods are the modified Muskat method25 and the
Arps-Smith method.26

relatively  short  tests.  The  disadvantages  are  the  need  for  accurate  fluid  property  estimates,  a

8.6 Diagnostic Plot
8.6.1 Introduction.  The diagnostic plot is a log-log plot of the pressure change and pressure
derivative (vertical axis) from a pressure transient test vs. elapsed time (horizontal axis). Fig.
8.43 shows an example. The diagnostic plot can be divided into three time regions: early, mid-
dle, and late. At the earliest times on a plot (the early-time region), wellbore and near-wellbore
effects dominate. These effects include wellbore storage, formation damage, partial penetration,
phase redistribution, and stimulation (hydraulic fractures or acidization). At intermediate times
(the middle-time region), a reservoir will ordinarily be infinite acting. For a homogeneous reser-
voir, the pressure derivative will be horizontal during this time region. Data in this region lead
to the most accurate estimates of formation permeability. At the latest times in a test (the late-
time region), boundary effects dom

are determined from the 
semilog plot and the two estimates of L from the pressure and time matches are 
obtained.  If the observed late-time response is indeed due to a single linear boundary 
these two estimates should be close in magnitude.  Thus the method has an internal 
consistency check.  Once L has been determined it may be necessary to refine 
the value of mQRC using Figure 11 and make a slight adjustment to the estimated 
value of k.  A large discrepancy between the pressure and time match estimates 
of L indicates that the model is not valid and the observed late-time effect has a 
different origin than a single fault.

In many cases the pressure response from a well test can be divided into three 
distinct periods when presented on a semilog plot as illustrated in Figure 11 for 
constant rate drawdown.  These are termed respectively:
       • Early time region  (ETR)
       • Middle time region (MTR)
       • Late time region  (LTR)

which the propagating pressure disturbance has not yet encountered any boundaries 
is known as the infinite-acting or transient flow regime.  It is this data which yields a 
straight line on the semilog plot, i.e. the pressure is varying with the log of time, and

8.3. SINGLE PHASE FLOW
8.3.1. Uniform Vertical Permeability
In order to appreciate the significance of pressure data in developed reservoirs it is 
useful to consider some relatively straight-forward situations which often arise in 
practice.  Consider first the case illustrated in Figure 6 where a new well - to become 
an edge water injector - has been drilled into the aquifer of a producing field.  Due to 
oil production from central wells and subsequent pressure depletion in the reservoir 
the aquifer is expanding into the oil zone as shown i.e. natural water drive is taking 
place.  Thus in the vicinity of the observation well water is moving updip and the 
local water flux has both a vertical and a horizontal component; from the point 
of view of WFT pressure interpretation it is the vertical component of the water 
flux, denoted uzw, which is important.  The vertical components of the flux and the 
potential gradient are related by D’Arcy’s law:
